voice: Fixed acoustic reference and speaker embedding from the local main.py test voice.

clips.text: An engine turns the pressure of burning fuel into rotation. We will build the moving parts first, then the valves, belts and fuel system. The cylinder block is the engine's main body. Pick up the largest hollow casting, the cylinder block. Its three large round holes guide the pistons. Place it on the main engine lift with these holes facing up. The open space underneath is where the crankshaft will fit.

A bearing lets a shaft turn with less rubbing. This smaller needle bearing contains many thin rollers inside a metal ring. Find the smaller of the two complete crankshaft bearing rings. Fit it into the smaller round support at one end of the block's open underside. Keep the ring's hole along the length of the block, where the crankshaft will run.

The larger needle bearing supports the other end of the crankshaft. Its rollers carry the load while allowing rotation. Find the larger complete bearing ring. Fit it into the larger round end support in the block's open underside. Its centre hole must line up with the smaller bearing at the other end.

The bearing shells are half rings. They form smooth surfaces between the crankshaft and the block. Look between the two end bearings. Place one curved shell in each of the four semicircular supports across the open underside. The hollow side of each shell faces the crankshaft. The other halves are fitted later.

The crankshaft changes the pistons' up-and-down movement into rotation. The smooth round sections are its bearing surfaces; the offset sections will connect to the rods. Pick up the long, unevenly shaped crankshaft. Lay it lengthwise in the open underside of the block. Centre its smooth bearing surfaces in the shells and rings you just fitted. Both ends project from the block.

A piston is a short metal cylinder. Burning gas pushes on its flat top, and the connecting rod passes this force to the crankshaft. We build this small unit separately before putting it in the engine. Find a piston on the nearby parts table. Put it on its separate work area with the flat top down and the hollow underside open toward you. You should be able to see the two holes through its sides.

The connecting rod links the piston to the crankshaft. Its small end pivots inside the piston; its large, split end will wrap around the crankshaft. Pick up the rod with a small hole at one end and a wide half-circle at the other. Put the small end inside the hollow piston. Line up its hole with the two holes through the piston sides. Leave the wide end outside.

The wrist pin is the hinge between the piston and its rod. It lets the rod change angle as the crankshaft turns. Find the short, smooth cylindrical pin. Slide it sideways through one piston hole, through the small hole in the connecting rod, and into the opposite piston hole. Centre the pin inside the piston before fitting its clips.

The two wrist-pin clips stop the hinge pin sliding out and scraping the cylinder wall. A circlip is a small split ring that sits in a groove. Fit one small split ring into the groove just inside each end of the piston pin hole. There are two clips, one on each side of the piston. Both sit outside the ends of the installed pin.

A stud is a threaded rod without a bolt head. These two studs will hold the connecting rod's separate cap when the piston is inside the engine. At the wide, open end of the connecting rod, find the two holes beside the half-circle. Fit one stud into each hole. Leave the separate curved cap off for now so the rod can pass around the crankshaft later.

The oil-control ring spreads a thin lubricating film and removes excess oil from the cylinder wall. It is different from the two rings that seal the gas pressure. Find the oil-control ring. Place it around the piston in the groove nearest the hollow underside and connecting rod. Describe the groove by the piston itself, not by its height above the floor, because the piston may be upside down.

The second ring helps scrape excess oil down the cylinder wall and supports the sealing work of the ring above it. Despite its name, oil control is an important job of this compression ring. Find the ring labelled second compression ring. Fit it around the piston in the middle of the three outside grooves. The oil-control ring is on one side of this groove; the flat piston top is on the other.

The top compression ring provides the first seal against the hot gas above the piston. With all three rings fitted, this piston unit is ready for the engine. Find the top compression ring and fit it into the outside groove closest to the flat piston top. Check the order from that flat top: top compression ring, second compression ring, then oil-control ring.

The three piston units work inside the block. Each connecting rod transfers the piston force to one offset section of the crankshaft. Pick up a completed piston-and-rod unit. Insert the rod end first into one of the three large cylinder holes. The flat piston top stays toward the cylinder-head side of the block, and the rod reaches the crankshaft underneath. Fit the other units into the remaining cylinders.

A connecting-rod cap completes the large round end of a rod. It surrounds a crankshaft bearing surface while still allowing the joint to turn. Look into the underside of the block. Find the open half-circle at the end of each connecting rod. Fit its curved cap against it, around the crankshaft, with the two cap holes over the rod's studs. Keep each cap with its own rod.

The nuts hold each connecting-rod cap onto its studs. The cap must stay attached while the engine turns. At each rod cap, find the two threaded stud ends projecting through the cap. Fit one nut on each end. Complete both nuts on all three rods. In this simulation, placing a fastener represents fitting it; it does not teach a real tightening torque.

The lower bearing shells complete the supports around the crankshaft. Their smooth curved faces reduce rubbing against the rotating shaft. Fit the four curved lower shells against the exposed halves of the crankshaft's main bearing surfaces. Each pairs with an upper shell already in the block. Leave their smooth, hollow faces toward the shaft.

The bedplate is the rigid lower frame that holds the crankshaft supports together. Find the large open frame, rather than the bowl-shaped sump. Place it across the underside of the block, over the lower bearing shells. Its long edges line up with the block edges and its bolt holes line up with the supports.

The long bedplate bolts clamp the lower support frame to the block so the crankshaft stays supported. Choose the bedplate bolts labelled M10 by 100. M10 identifies the thread size; 100 is the length in millimetres. Fit them through the deeper bolt holes of the bedplate into the block. Keep the shorter M8 bolts for the next group.

The smaller bedplate bolts secure the remaining attachment points around the lower frame. Choose the bolts labelled M8 by 80. Insert them through the remaining bedplate bolt holes into the block. Their heads rest on the outside face of the frame. Do not use the M8 head-cover bolts from a later chapter.

The oil sump is the bowl that collects lubricating oil beneath the engine. Oil helps moving parts slide without damaging one another. Find the large bowl-shaped sump on the parts table. Place it in its separate work area with the open side accessible. We will add the plate inside the bowl before attaching the whole sump to the engine.

The baffle is a plate that reduces oil sloshing inside the sump as the engine or vehicle moves. Lower the flat baffle plate into the open sump. Its four small screw holes line up with the four raised attachment points inside the bowl. Keep the broad plate inside the bowl, below its outer rim.

The four short screws hold the baffle in the sump. Choose the small M4 by 5 screws for the baffle. Put one through each of the four holes in the plate into the support beneath it. After all four are fitted, the sump and baffle can be carried together.

The completed sump closes the bottom of the engine and provides its oil reservoir. Pick up the whole sump-and-baffle unit. Bring its open rim against the underside of the bedplate. The bowl projects away from the engine and the baffle stays inside. Line up the perimeter holes before fitting the fasteners.

The large sump fastener fits a much wider threaded opening than the smaller attachment bolts. Its diameter helps you distinguish its position from the holes around the rim. Choose the M16 by 55 bolt. Find the large opening on the bottom region of the sump, toward the flywheel end, rather than a small rim hole. Place its threaded end into that opening and leave its head outside.

The short bolt secures one of the shallow attachment points on the sump rim. Choose the M8 by 30 bolt. Find the sump rim corner on the intake side nearest the flywheel. Insert the threaded end through this shallow support toward the engine, leaving the head on the outer face.

The set of bolts clamps the sump rim against the engine at equal-depth attachment points. Choose the four M8 by 35 bolts. Their four holes run across the timing end of the sump rim, the end opposite the flywheel. Place one bolt in each hole with its head outside the rim.

The sump has supports of different depths, so its mounting bolts are not all the same length. Choose the M8 by 40 bolt. Find the sump rim corner on the exhaust side nearest the flywheel. Fit the bolt through this support toward the engine and seat its head against the outside face.

The bolt reaches through a deeper sump support than the shorter bolts you have just placed. Choose the M8 by 45 bolt. On the exhaust-side edge of the sump, move inward from the flywheel corner to the next mounting support. Fit the bolt through that support, with its head outside.

The longest sump bolts pass through the deepest attachment supports to reach the engine above. Choose the three long M8 by 80 sump bolts. Two go through deep supports on opposite long sides, toward the timing half of the sump. The third goes through the deeper intake-side support nearer the flywheel. Keep all heads on the outside of the supports.

The flywheel is a heavy disc that stores rotational energy. It helps the crankshaft turn smoothly between the pushes from the pistons. Find the large round disc. Fit its centre onto the exposed crankshaft end opposite the timing pulleys. Its flat mounting face sits against the crankshaft flange, and the ring of small bolt holes surrounds the shaft centre.

The retaining plate spreads the force of the flywheel bolts around the centre of the disc. Find the smaller flat round plate with several bolt holes. Place it over the centre of the installed flywheel. Line up its holes with the holes in the flywheel and crankshaft flange underneath.

The six bolts lock the flywheel and retaining plate to the crankshaft. Choose the six M10 by 20 flywheel bolts. Place one through each hole in the small retaining plate at the centre of the flywheel. The bolt heads face away from the engine.

The cylinder head closes the tops of the cylinders. Its valves let fresh air in and exhaust gas out. Each of the three chambers has four valve openings. Find the long rectangular cylinder head and place it on its separate work area. Look at the face with three shallow chamber shapes. The small holes inside each chamber are where the valve stems pass through. We will build the valves here before moving the head onto the engine.

An exhaust valve opens to let burnt gas leave a cylinder. It looks like a long thin stem with a flat round head at one end. Choose the exhaust valves, using their part labels to distinguish them from intake valves. From the chamber face of the loose cylinder head, slide each stem into an exhaust guide hole. The round valve head stays in the chamber and closes against its circular seat. Fit the exhaust pair in each chamber.

An intake valve opens to let fresh air enter a cylinder. When it closes, it helps seal the gas above the piston. Choose the intake valves. From the chamber face of the head, slide their stems through the remaining intake guide holes. Keep the wide round heads on the chamber side. Each chamber now has two intake and two exhaust valves.

The spring seat is a thin metal ring that gives the valve spring a firm surface to push against. It protects the cylinder head from the spring end. On the opposite side from the flat valve faces, find a valve stem sticking out of its short guide tube. Slide the thin spring-seat ring down around that tube until it rests flat on the cylinder head.

The stem seal controls how much oil can run down the valve stem. Too much oil entering the air passage would be burned in the cylinder. Find the tiny cap-shaped seal with a hole through it. Slide it over the exposed valve stem and down onto the top of the guide tube, inside the spring-seat ring. Keep the hole centred on the stem.

The valve spring pushes the valve closed after the camshaft releases it. It must surround the same stem as the seat and seal. Pick up the coil spring. Slide it over the valve stem and seal. Rest its lower end on the flat spring-seat ring already on the head. The stem remains visible through the centre of the spring.

The retainer is the small cap that holds the top of the valve spring. It will be locked to the stem by two tiny keeper halves. Find the cap-shaped spring retainer. Place it over the top end of the spring, with the valve stem through its centre hole. The wider face covers the spring end; leave the groove near the stem tip accessible for the keepers.

The two keeper halves lock into the stem groove and hold the spring retainer in place. Together they form a small collar around the stem. Find the two tiny half-collars. Put one on each side of the groove near the valve-stem tip, inside the retainer's centre opening. Both halves belong around the same stem. This completes that valve's spring stack.

The completed head brings the valves and combustion chambers together with the pistons below. Pick up the entire finished cylinder-head unit. Place its chamber face against the top of the block. Line up the three chambers with the three large cylinder holes. The springs and camshaft supports face away from the block.

The long head bolts clamp the cylinder head to the block so the joint can resist the pressure inside the cylinders. Choose the eight cylinder-head bolts. Insert them into the long holes through the head, alongside the valve groups. Their threaded ends reach into the block; their heads stay on the outer head face. Fill all eight positions.

The camshaft bearings let the two valve-operating shafts rotate smoothly above the valves. Find the eight small needle-bearing rings. Fit them in the round supports running lengthwise along the open top of the cylinder head. Four supports belong to each camshaft. Keep each ring's hole along the shaft direction.

The exhaust camshaft controls when the exhaust valves open. Its raised bumps, called lobes, press the valve mechanism as the shaft rotates. Choose the shaft labelled exhaust camshaft. Lay it lengthwise in the bearing row above the exhaust valves. Its smooth sections rest in the bearings, its lobes sit over the valve positions, and its pulley end projects from the timing end of the head.

The intake camshaft controls when fresh air can enter through the intake valves. It is separate from the exhaust camshaft. Choose the intake camshaft and lay it in the other bearing row, above the intake valves. Put its smooth bearing sections in the supports and its pulley end at the same end of the head as the exhaust camshaft pulley end.

The front cover closes the timing end of the engine. It surrounds the shaft end without preventing it from rotating. Find the shaped front cover. Place it against the block end opposite the flywheel. Line up its large opening with the projecting crankshaft and its outline with the end face of the block.

A pulley key is a small metal piece that stops a pulley hub slipping around its shaft. Find the two small camshaft keys. Fit one lengthwise into the narrow slot on each projecting camshaft end. Part of the key remains above the shaft surface so it can engage the slot inside the hub.

The hub is the centre piece that connects a camshaft to its outer belt pulley. Slide one hub over each keyed camshaft end. Turn the hub so the slot inside its centre hole passes over the key. Seat the hub against the shaft shoulder, leaving its centre opening accessible for the washer and bolt.

A washer spreads the bolt's clamping force across the hub. These washers must go inside before the bolts and outer pulleys hide them. Find the two camshaft pulley washers. Place one in the centre recess of each installed hub, with its hole lined up with the hole in the shaft end. The washer lies flat inside the recess.

The bolts hold the hubs tightly against the camshafts. The keys transmit the turning force; the bolts prevent the hubs coming off. Fit one M12 by 45 bolt through the washer in each camshaft hub. Point the thread into the shaft end. The bolt head rests against the washer inside the hub, before the outer pulley is added.

The crankshaft key makes the lower belt pulley rotate with the crankshaft. Find the crankshaft pulley key. Fit it lengthwise in the narrow slot on the crankshaft end projecting through the front cover. Leave its outer edge exposed so it engages the pulley slot.

The two camshaft pulleys receive motion from the timing belt. Their teeth keep the belt from slipping over them. Fit the two large toothed camshaft pulleys over the secured hubs at the top of the timing end. Their centre openings surround the hub centres, and their mounting holes line up with the holes in the hubs.

The crankshaft pulley drives the timing belt from the rotating crankshaft. Fit the lower timing pulley over the crankshaft end below the two camshaft pulleys. Line up the slot inside the pulley with the key on the shaft. Slide the pulley inward until its rear face meets the shaft shoulder.

The washer spreads the force from the large retaining nut over the crankshaft pulley. Place the crankshaft pulley washer over the exposed shaft end. Seat it flat against the outside face of the lower pulley, with the threaded end of the shaft still projecting through its centre.

The outer pulley bolts fasten the toothed camshaft pulleys to their hubs. Choose the M8 by 35 outer-pulley bolts. Put them through the small mounting holes around the centres of the two upper timing pulleys. Their heads stay on the outside faces of the pulleys.

The large nut holds the lower timing pulley on the crankshaft. Find the M22 nut. Fit it onto the threaded crankshaft end projecting through the washer at the centre of the lower pulley. It sits against the washer, not directly against the pulley.

An idler is a guide pulley. This plate supports the shafts of the two timing-belt idlers. Find the timing-idler mounting plate. Place it on the front face of the engine beside the timing pulleys. Its flat back faces the engine; the two positions for the short idler shafts face outward.

The mounting-plate screws keep the belt-guide supports fixed relative to the engine. Fit the four M8 by 20 screws through the mounting holes in the idler plate into the engine face behind it. Their heads remain on the outer face of the plate.

The short shafts hold the idler pulleys in position while the pulleys turn on bearings. Fit one short idler shaft into each of the two shaft openings on the mounting plate. The shafts project outward, parallel to the crankshaft. Keep their retaining-ring grooves accessible.

The inner shaft clips set the inward limit for each idler. They must be fitted before the pulley hides these grooves. Fit one split ring into the groove nearest the plate on each idler shaft. These clips go around the outside of the shafts. Leave the outer grooves empty until the complete idlers are installed.

An idler guides the belt without driving an engine shaft. Its internal bearings let it spin on a fixed support. Find the first small timing-idler pulley. Place it in its separate work area with its large centre opening accessible. We will put two bearings inside this opening before carrying the pulley to the engine.

The two ball bearings let the timing-idler pulley spin around its stationary shaft with little friction. Fit both bearing rings inside the centre opening of the first idler pulley. Keep their small centre holes in line. The outer bearing rings sit inside the pulley; the shaft will later pass through their centre holes.

The retaining rings stop the bearings sliding out of the idler pulley. Fit one split retaining ring into the groove inside each end of the first pulley opening, outside the bearings. These rings fit inside the pulley, unlike the clips that fit around the engine's idler shafts.

The second timing idler guides another section of the same belt. It needs its own pair of bearings and retaining rings. Place the second small timing-idler pulley in its separate work area. Keep its centre opening accessible for the bearings. Leave the first completed idler in its own area until both are ready to mount.

The ball bearings support the second idler on its fixed shaft. Fit both bearing rings into the second pulley's centre opening. Keep their small holes in line along the pulley axis, ready to slide over the idler shaft.

The second pulley's internal clips retain its two bearings. Fit one split ring into the groove inside each end of the second pulley opening. Each ring sits outside a bearing and prevents it sliding out. The second idler is now a complete unit.

The finished idlers can now turn freely while their support shafts stay fixed. Slide each completed idler onto one of the two shafts on the timing-idler plate. Pass the shaft through the bearing holes. Push the unit inward until it reaches the inner shaft clip already fitted, leaving the outer groove exposed.

The outer shaft clips keep the complete idlers from sliding off their supports. Fit one split ring around the exposed outer groove of each idler shaft. The pulley is now held between an inner and outer clip. Do not put these clips inside the pulley opening.

The timing belt keeps the crankshaft and camshafts moving in step, so valves open at the right point in each piston stroke. Incorrect timing could let a piston hit a valve. Find the toothed timing belt. Place it around the lower crankshaft pulley, the two upper camshaft pulleys and the small guide idlers on the front of the engine. Its toothed face engages the toothed pulleys. This model shows the fitted route, not a real timing or tension adjustment.

The cylinder-head cover encloses the camshafts, keeps dirt out and helps keep oil inside. Place the long cover over the two camshafts on top of the cylinder head. Its open face goes toward the shafts. Align its outer rim and mounting holes with the rim of the head beneath it.

The bolts clamp the cover to the cylinder head. Choose the cover bolts from this chapter. Insert them into the holes around the edge of the installed head cover, with their heads outside. Keep them separate from the earlier bolts that hold the head to the block.

Fuel injectors deliver controlled amounts of fuel into the engine. Each cylinder has its own injector. Find the three slim injector bodies. Put one nozzle-first into each injector opening along the head. Leave their upper fuel connections outside, in a row, so the fuel rail can connect to all three.

The fuel rail distributes fuel to all three injectors from a shared supply. Find the long rail with three connections. Place it across the tops of the installed injectors. Line up one rail connection with each injector's upper connection, without crossing the rail diagonally.

The two screws keep the fuel rail fixed so its connections stay aligned with the injectors. Fit the two M6 by 10 rail screws through the rail's mounting tabs into the supports below. The screw heads rest on the tabs, clear of the three injector connections.

The return line provides a route for fuel returning from the fuel system rather than entering the cylinders. Find the narrow fuel return line. Follow the small return connections beside the injectors and fuel rail. Place the line along those connections, with its open ends facing the connection points, rather than the injector nozzles.

Some gas passes the piston rings into the lower engine. The breather provides a controlled way for this gas to leave, instead of pressure building inside the crankcase. Find the small breather housing. Place its flat mounting face against the breather opening on the engine, with its hose outlet pointing outward. Its two screw holes line up with the holes beside that opening.

The screws hold the breather housing against its mounting face. Fit the two breather-housing screws through the holes beside the housing outlet into the engine. Keep the hose outlet clear for the next part.

The breather hose carries crankcase gas from the breather housing toward the intake system. Find the curved hose. Connect one end over the breather outlet and the other over the intake-side connection. Follow the hose's existing bend along the engine; do not place it across the belt pulleys.

The exhaust manifold collects burnt gas from the cylinders. This model joins it to the turbocharger housing, where exhaust energy will help pump more fresh air into the engine. Find the casting with several exhaust branches and a rounded turbo housing. Place its branch openings against the row of exhaust ports on the side of the cylinder head. The rounded turbo housing projects outward from the engine.

The screws secure the exhaust manifold so it stays attached to the cylinder head. Fit the four manifold screws through the mounting holes around the exhaust branches into the head. Their heads sit on the outside of the manifold flange, the flat edge surrounding the ports.

The turbo shaft rotates very quickly. Its two small bearings support it inside the central housing. Find the two small turbo bearing rings. Fit them into the centre passage through the turbo housing, one at each bearing position. Keep their holes in a straight line for the shaft.

The turbo shaft links the exhaust-driven turbine to the fresh-air compressor. When one wheel turns, the other turns with it. Slide the thin turbo rotor shaft through both bearing holes in the centre of the turbo housing. Leave a shaft end exposed on each side for the two different wheels.

The small clips retain the turbo shaft at its intended position through the bearings. Fit the two small retaining rings into the grooves on the turbo shaft beside its bearing positions. Keep both exposed shaft ends clear for the compressor and turbine wheels.

The compressor wheel draws in and compresses fresh air. Denser air lets the cylinders receive more oxygen. Choose the bladed wheel labelled compressor. Fit its centre hole onto the turbo shaft at the fresh-air intake side, opposite the exhaust outlet. The blade assembly stays inside the air-side housing opening.

The turbine wheel takes energy from the hot exhaust gas. It drives the compressor through their shared shaft. Choose the wheel labelled turbine. Fit it onto the other turbo shaft end, on the exhaust-manifold and outlet side. Do not swap it with the compressor wheel; they handle different gas paths.

The small fasteners secure the two turbo wheels to the shared shaft. Fit one M4 fastener at the centre of each installed turbo wheel, into its shaft-end attachment. The fastener holds the wheel on the shaft without covering its blades.

The exhaust outlet carries gas away after it passes the turbine. The catalyst housing contains the area used for exhaust treatment. Find the outlet and catalyst housing. Join its round inlet to the exhaust-side opening of the turbocharger. Bring the two circular edges together; the band clamp will wrap around this joint next.

The band clamp squeezes the two round exhaust edges together to hold the joint closed. Place the open band around the circular joint between the turbo housing and exhaust outlet. Its tightening tabs stay together on the outside where the clamp bolt can pass through them. Fit the band before its bolt.

The bolt tightens the outlet clamp around the exhaust joint. Find the M8 by 12 clamp bolt. Put it through the clamp's tightening tabs, across the gap in the band. It belongs in the clamp, not in the centre of the exhaust opening.

The intake manifold shares incoming air between the three cylinders. It is the fresh-air counterpart of the exhaust manifold. Find the branching intake casting. Fit its row of outlets against the intake ports on the other side of the cylinder head from the exhaust manifold. Its larger common inlet remains open for the intake pipe connection.

The intake pipe fitting joins the incoming air pipe to the intake manifold. Find the intake pipe fitting. Place its connecting end into the large common inlet of the intake manifold. Its other end points toward the incoming air route, away from the three cylinder-head ports.

A union joins two pipe sections so their flow passages form one continuous route. Fit the intake pipe union onto the exposed pipe connection you just installed. Align the centre openings and bring the joining faces together. It continues the air path into the manifold.

The external tube connects two service points along the engine. The CAD model does not identify the fluid it carries, so we will describe its route without assigning it a fuel or oil function. Find the long, narrow bent service tube. Follow its bends along the outside of the engine and line up both open ends with their connection points. It lies alongside the engine rather than around the rotating belts.

Accessory brackets support equipment attached to the engine. The upper bracket establishes the upper attachment position. Find the upper accessory bracket. Fit its flat engine-side face to the upper accessory mounting points beside the belt end. Its projecting supports face away from the block. Fit this bracket before the lower one.

The lower bracket provides the second support for the accessories. Together the brackets hold equipment in line with its belt. Place the lower accessory bracket beneath the upper bracket. Bring its flat mounting face against the lower attachment points on the engine and keep its projecting supports on the same outside face as the upper bracket.

A spacer fills a deliberate gap so tightening a mounting connection does not pull the parts out of line. Choose spacer A. At the timing end, put it in the accessory bracket gap on the exhaust side of the engine centre. Line its hole up with the mounting holes so a fastener can pass through the bracket and spacer.

Spacer B sets the distance at the other bracket attachment. Different spacers are not interchangeable just because both have a hole. Choose spacer B. At the timing end, put it in the other bracket gap, on the intake side of the engine centre. Line its centre hole up with the bracket mounting holes. Its two ends set the distance between the adjoining supports.

The alternator turns mechanical rotation into electrical energy to supply equipment and charge a battery. Find the alternator, the vented body with a small projecting shaft. Place its mounting ears between the accessory supports and spacers. Its shaft faces the belt end of the engine, where its pulley will be fitted next.

The starter motor uses electrical power to turn the engine when starting. Once the engine runs, combustion keeps it turning. Find the starter motor, the compact cylindrical unit. Fit its mounting flange at the starter position beside the flywheel end of the engine. Its drive end faces the flywheel so it can turn the engine during starting.

The alternator pulley receives rotation from the accessory belt and turns the alternator shaft. Fit the small alternator pulley over the shaft projecting from the alternator. Its grooved belt surface faces outward in the same belt plane as the other accessory pulleys.

The accessory-idler shaft is a fixed support for a free-turning belt guide. Fit the short accessory-idler shaft into its opening on the accessory support. Let it project outward toward the accessory belt. The two clip grooves must remain accessible for the inner clip, pulley and outer clip.

The inner clip stops the accessory idler sliding too far inward on its support shaft. Fit the split shaft ring into the groove nearest the accessory support. This clip goes around the shaft before the assembled pulley covers that area. Leave the outer groove empty for now.

The accessory idler guides the accessory belt without driving a separate machine. Place the small accessory-idler pulley in its separate work area. Keep its centre opening accessible. It will receive two bearings and two internal clips before it is carried to the engine.

The two ball bearings let the accessory pulley turn smoothly on its fixed shaft. Fit both bearing rings inside the accessory pulley's centre opening. Their small centre holes line up along the pulley axis. The shaft will later pass through these holes.

The internal clips keep the bearings inside the accessory pulley. Fit one split ring into the groove inside each end of the pulley opening. Each clip sits outside a bearing. These clips belong inside the pulley, not around the support shaft.

The completed accessory idler is now ready to guide the belt. Slide the whole idler unit over the accessory-idler shaft through its bearing holes. Move it inward until it reaches the inner shaft clip already fitted. The shaft's outer clip groove should remain exposed.

The outer shaft clip prevents the accessory idler sliding off the engine. Fit the split ring into the exposed outer groove of the idler shaft, just beyond the pulley bearing. The pulley is now held between the two shaft clips.

An electric motor converts electrical energy into rotation. Find the complete motor unit. Place its mounting feet on the motor supports beside the accessory assembly. Line up the two mounting holes in its feet with the holes through the supports before adding the long bolts.

The long bolts pass through the motor feet and supports to hold the motor in position. Fit the two motor mounting bolts through the aligned holes in the motor feet and supports. Leave their threaded ends projecting from the opposite side for the nuts.

The nuts complete the motor's mounting connections by clamping the supports between the bolt heads and nuts. Put one motor mounting nut onto each projecting bolt end on the opposite side of the supports from the bolt heads. Both mounting connections must be complete before fitting the belt.

The accessory belt transfers rotation from the engine to belt-driven equipment, including the alternator. Unlike the timing belt, its main job is to drive accessories, not time the valves. Place the accessory belt around the accessory pulleys and guide idler on the outside of the engine. Keep it in their common belt plane. You have now connected the engine's internal motion, gas flow, fuel supply and external equipment into one assembly.

A bearing lets the guide pulley rotate freely on a fixed shaft. Remove only the parts needed to reach the faulty bearing, replace it, then rebuild the same connections. Set removed parts aside using the drop control; on PC this is G.

We will replace one bearing inside a timing-belt guide pulley. A worn bearing can stop the pulley turning freely. First find the toothed belt on the end opposite the flywheel. Lift it off the large pulleys and small idlers, then set it on the parts table. This gives access to the faulty idler.

Find the first small timing idler, labelled timing idler one. The split ring on the exposed end of its shaft stops the pulley sliding off. Remove this outer ring and set it aside. Leave the inner ring, behind the pulley, on the shaft.

Slide the whole first idler off its fixed shaft. Carry it to the small work platform and set it down with its centre opening accessible. We are removing the pulley and its internal bearings together, not removing the shaft from the engine.

Look inside the pulley opening. The two rings in grooves inside this opening hold the bearings in the pulley. Remove the first internal retaining ring and set it aside for reuse. These internal rings are different from the ring you removed from the engine shaft.

Remove the second internal retaining ring from the other end of the pulley opening. Set it aside with the first. Both bearings are now free of their retaining rings, so we can reach the damaged bearing without forcing it past a clip.

Remove the outer bearing ring from the pulley centre and set it aside for reuse. Its balls let the pulley rotate around the fixed shaft. This bearing is still good; removing it gives access to the inner bearing that needs replacement.
Remove the faulty inner bearing from the now-open pulley centre. Set this damaged bearing aside separately. We will use a new bearing of the same size instead of putting the faulty one back.

Pick up the part labelled New replacement timing idler bearing. Fit it into the empty inner bearing position inside the pulley centre. Its outer ring seats in the pulley, and its small centre hole lines up with the pulley axis.

Pick up the original good outer bearing. Refit it into the remaining seat at the outer end of the pulley opening. The two small bearing holes must line up so the engine's fixed shaft can pass through both.

Refit the first internal split ring into its groove inside the pulley opening, just outside the bearing. It stops the bearing sliding out. Keep the centre opening clear; the ring sits at the edge of the opening.

Refit the second internal split ring in the groove at the other end of the opening. Both bearings are now retained. The rebuilt idler contains one new bearing and one reused bearing, held by the original two internal rings.

Pick up the rebuilt idler as one unit. Slide its bearing holes over the original shaft on the engine's timing-idler plate. Move it inward until it reaches the inner shaft ring that you left in place. Leave the outer shaft groove visible.
Refit the outer shaft clip into the exposed groove just beyond the pulley. The two shaft clips now keep the whole idler on the engine, while its internal bearings allow it to turn.

Refit the toothed timing belt around the lower crankshaft pulley, the two upper camshaft pulleys and the small guide idlers. You have replaced the faulty bearing and reused the good parts. The belt again links piston movement to valve movement. This simulation shows the fitted route; real timing and tension checks require engine-specific instructions.
Chapter complete. Your section is assembled. Continue to the next chapter when you are ready.
Repair complete. The replacement bearing is fitted and the timing drive is rebuilt.

The cylinder block is the engine's main body. Its three cylindrical bores guide the pistons, while its lower structure supports the crankshaft.
A bearing lets a shaft turn with less rubbing. This smaller needle bearing contains many thin rollers inside a metal ring.
The larger needle bearing supports the other end of the crankshaft. Its rollers carry the load while allowing rotation.
The bearing shells are half rings. They form smooth surfaces between the crankshaft and the block.
The crankshaft changes the pistons' up-and-down movement into rotation. The smooth round sections are its bearing surfaces; the offset sections will connect to the rods.
A piston is a short metal cylinder. Burning gas pushes on its flat top, and the connecting rod passes this force to the crankshaft.
The connecting rod links the piston to the crankshaft. Its small end pivots inside the piston; its large, split end will wrap around the crankshaft.
The wrist pin is the hinge between the piston and its rod. It lets the rod change angle as the crankshaft turns.
The two wrist-pin clips stop the hinge pin sliding out and scraping the cylinder wall. A circlip is a small split ring that sits in a groove.
A stud is a threaded rod without a bolt head. These two studs will hold the connecting rod's separate cap when the piston is inside the engine.
The oil-control ring spreads a thin lubricating film and removes excess oil from the cylinder wall. It is different from the two rings that seal the gas pressure.
The second ring helps scrape excess oil down the cylinder wall and supports the sealing work of the ring above it. Despite its name, oil control is an important job of this compression ring.
The top compression ring provides the first seal against the hot gas above the piston. It reduces gas escaping between the piston and the cylinder wall.
The three piston units work inside the block. Each connecting rod transfers the piston force to one offset section of the crankshaft.
A connecting-rod cap completes the large round end of a rod. It surrounds a crankshaft bearing surface while still allowing the joint to turn.
The nuts hold each connecting-rod cap onto its studs. The cap must stay attached while the engine turns.
The lower bearing shells complete the supports around the crankshaft. Their smooth curved faces reduce rubbing against the rotating shaft.
The bedplate is the rigid lower frame that holds the crankshaft supports together.
The long bedplate bolts clamp the lower support frame to the block so the crankshaft stays supported.
The smaller bedplate bolts secure the remaining attachment points around the lower frame.
The oil sump is the bowl that collects lubricating oil beneath the engine. Oil helps moving parts slide without damaging one another.
The baffle is a plate that reduces oil sloshing inside the sump as the engine or vehicle moves.
The four short screws hold the baffle in the sump.
The completed sump closes the bottom of the engine and provides its oil reservoir.
The large sump fastener fits a wider threaded opening in the oil sump than the smaller fasteners around its rim.
The short bolt secures one of the shallow attachment points on the sump rim.
The set of bolts clamps the sump rim against the engine at equal-depth attachment points.
The sump has supports of different depths, so its mounting bolts are not all the same length.
The longer sump bolt reaches through a deep support to clamp the oil sump to the engine.
The longest sump bolts pass through the deepest attachment supports to reach the engine above.
The flywheel is a heavy disc that stores rotational energy. It helps the crankshaft turn smoothly between the pushes from the pistons.
The retaining plate spreads the force of the flywheel bolts around the centre of the disc.
The six bolts lock the flywheel and retaining plate to the crankshaft.
The cylinder head closes the tops of the cylinders. Its valves let fresh air in and exhaust gas out. Each of the three chambers has four valve openings.
An exhaust valve opens to let burnt gas leave a cylinder. It looks like a long thin stem with a flat round head at one end.
An intake valve opens to let fresh air enter a cylinder. When it closes, it helps seal the gas above the piston.
The spring seat is a thin metal ring that gives the valve spring a firm surface to push against. It protects the cylinder head from the spring end.
The stem seal controls how much oil can run down the valve stem. Too much oil entering the air passage would be burned in the cylinder.
The valve spring pushes the valve closed after the camshaft releases it. The spring surrounds the valve stem and presses against the spring seat and retainer.
The retainer is the small cap that holds the top of the valve spring. It will be locked to the stem by two tiny keeper halves.
The two keeper halves lock into the stem groove and hold the spring retainer in place. Together they form a small collar around the stem.
The completed head brings the valves and combustion chambers together with the pistons below.
The long head bolts clamp the cylinder head to the block so the joint can resist the pressure inside the cylinders.
The camshaft bearings let the two valve-operating shafts rotate smoothly above the valves.
The exhaust camshaft controls when the exhaust valves open. Its raised bumps, called lobes, press the valve mechanism as the shaft rotates.
The intake camshaft controls when fresh air can enter through the intake valves. It is separate from the exhaust camshaft.
The front cover closes the timing end of the engine. It surrounds the shaft end without preventing it from rotating.
A pulley key is a small metal piece that stops a pulley hub slipping around its shaft.
The hub is the centre piece that connects a camshaft to its outer belt pulley.
A camshaft pulley washer spreads the retaining bolt's clamping force across the hub and protects its contact surface.
The bolts hold the hubs tightly against the camshafts. The keys transmit the turning force; the bolts prevent the hubs coming off.
The crankshaft key makes the lower belt pulley rotate with the crankshaft.
The two camshaft pulleys receive motion from the timing belt. Their teeth keep the belt from slipping over them.
The crankshaft pulley drives the timing belt from the rotating crankshaft.
The washer spreads the force from the large retaining nut over the crankshaft pulley.
The outer pulley bolts fasten the toothed camshaft pulleys to their hubs.
The large nut holds the lower timing pulley on the crankshaft.
An idler is a guide pulley. This plate supports the shafts of the two timing-belt idlers.
The mounting-plate screws keep the belt-guide supports fixed relative to the engine.
The short shafts hold the idler pulleys in position while the pulleys turn on bearings.
The inner shaft clips set the inward limit for each idler. Their grooves hold the clips at a fixed position on the support shaft.
An idler guides the belt without driving an engine shaft. Its internal bearings let it spin on a fixed support.
The two ball bearings let the timing-idler pulley spin around its stationary shaft with little friction.
The retaining rings stop the bearings sliding out of the idler pulley.
The second timing idler guides another section of the same belt. It needs its own pair of bearings and retaining rings.
The ball bearings support the second idler on its fixed shaft.
The second pulley's internal clips retain its two bearings.
The finished idlers can now turn freely while their support shafts stay fixed.
The outer shaft clips keep the complete idlers from sliding off their supports.
The timing belt keeps the crankshaft and camshafts moving in step, so valves open at the right point in each piston stroke. Incorrect timing could let a piston hit a valve.
The cylinder-head cover encloses the camshafts, keeps dirt out and helps keep oil inside.
The bolts clamp the cover to the cylinder head.
Fuel injectors deliver controlled amounts of fuel into the engine. Each cylinder has its own injector.
The fuel rail distributes fuel to all three injectors from a shared supply.
The two screws keep the fuel rail fixed so its connections stay aligned with the injectors.
The return line provides a route for fuel returning from the fuel system rather than entering the cylinders.
Some gas passes the piston rings into the lower engine. The breather provides a controlled way for this gas to leave, instead of pressure building inside the crankcase.
The screws hold the breather housing against its mounting face.
The breather hose carries crankcase gas from the breather housing toward the intake system.
The exhaust manifold collects burnt gas from the cylinders. This model joins it to the turbocharger housing, where exhaust energy will help pump more fresh air into the engine.
The screws secure the exhaust manifold so it stays attached to the cylinder head.
The turbo shaft rotates very quickly. Its two small bearings support it inside the central housing.
The turbo shaft links the exhaust-driven turbine to the fresh-air compressor. When one wheel turns, the other turns with it.
The small clips retain the turbo shaft at its intended position through the bearings.
The compressor wheel draws in and compresses fresh air. Denser air lets the cylinders receive more oxygen.
The turbine wheel takes energy from the hot exhaust gas. It drives the compressor through their shared shaft.
The small fasteners secure the two turbo wheels to the shared shaft.
The exhaust outlet carries gas away after it passes the turbine. The catalyst housing contains the area used for exhaust treatment.
The band clamp squeezes the two round exhaust edges together to hold the joint closed.
The bolt tightens the outlet clamp around the exhaust joint.
The intake manifold shares incoming air between the three cylinders. It is the fresh-air counterpart of the exhaust manifold.
The intake pipe fitting joins the incoming air pipe to the intake manifold.
A union joins two pipe sections so their flow passages form one continuous route.
The external tube connects two service points along the engine. The fluid circuit is not identified in the supplied CAD model.
Accessory brackets support equipment attached to the engine. The upper bracket establishes the upper attachment position.
The lower bracket provides the second support for the accessories. Together the brackets hold equipment in line with its belt.
A spacer fills a deliberate gap so tightening a mounting connection does not pull the parts out of line.
Spacer B sets the distance at the other bracket attachment. Different spacers are not interchangeable just because both have a hole.
The alternator turns mechanical rotation into electrical energy to supply equipment and charge a battery.
The starter motor uses electrical power to turn the engine when starting. Once the engine runs, combustion keeps it turning.
The alternator pulley receives rotation from the accessory belt and turns the alternator shaft.
The accessory-idler shaft is a fixed support for a free-turning belt guide.
The inner clip stops the accessory idler sliding too far inward on its support shaft.
The accessory idler guides the accessory belt without driving a separate machine.
The two ball bearings let the accessory pulley turn smoothly on its fixed shaft.
The internal clips keep the bearings inside the accessory pulley.
The accessory idler guides the drive belt. Its bearings let the pulley rotate around a fixed support shaft.
The outer shaft clip prevents the accessory idler sliding off the engine.
An electric motor converts electrical energy into rotation.
The long bolts pass through the motor feet and supports to hold the motor in position.
The nuts complete the motor's mounting connections by clamping the supports between the bolt heads and nuts.
The accessory belt transfers rotation from the engine to belt-driven equipment, including the alternator. Unlike the timing belt, its main job is to drive accessories, not time the valves.

An engine turns energy from burning fuel into rotation. The pistons slide inside the cylinders. Connecting rods link the pistons to the crankshaft, which turns as the pistons move. The belt drives the camshafts at half the crankshaft speed. Cam lobes open the valves, and springs close them. Follow the nearest cylinder through four strokes.

During the intake stroke, the piston moves down and the intake valves open. Fresh air enters the space above the piston. Blue represents the incoming air. The exhaust valves stay closed so the air follows the intake passage.

During the compression stroke, the piston moves up with both sets of valves closed. The trapped air is squeezed into a smaller space, increasing its pressure and temperature. Gold represents the compressed air near the top of the cylinder.

During the power stroke, fuel burns in the hot compressed air. Orange represents the hot gas expanding and pushing the piston down. The connecting rod transfers that push to the crankshaft. The crankshaft delivers rotation to the rest of the machine.

During the exhaust stroke, the exhaust valves open and the piston moves up. Used gas leaves the cylinder through the exhaust passage. Grey represents the outgoing gas. The intake valves then open for another cycle. Four strokes take two complete crankshaft turns and one camshaft turn.

Walk with W, A, S and D, and look around with the mouse. Hold Shift to walk faster. Space jumps, and Control crouches. The large table holds your loose parts; the lifts hold the engine and smaller assemblies.

Aim at a loose part and click to pick it up. Click another matching part to carry several of the same type, one pickup at a time. The inventory shows the quantity. Different sizes of screw cannot share that stack. Press G to put down the held part.

In Easy difficulty, pick up the part, aim at its visible ghost, and click to fit it. Medium and Hard also use Q to switch between carrying and placement. In placement mode, hold the right mouse button to adjust the part. T switches between moving and rotating. Hard requires the correct orientation.

Point at a lift's red lever, hold the left mouse button, and drag up or down to change its height. Release to stop. Press the red flip button to turn that lift's assembly over. The hatch opens while the assembly turns below the floor. Follow a flip instruction before fitting the next part.

V toggles the arrow to the next part, then its fitting position after pickup. H toggles ghost hints. R replays the current explanation. N installs the next part for you. Tab opens chapters, and Escape pauses the workshop. Settings contains volume, placement difficulty and the full controls.

Allow camera access, then move the phone slowly over a clear, well-lit surface. Tap Place Engine when a surface is found. The engine floats at working height. If AR is unavailable, choose phone view to use the same assembly without a camera.

Choose a part from the cards at the bottom, then tap its visible glowing target to fit it. Cards follow the assembly order and disappear after placement. Any piston may be started first, but finish that piston before starting another. Smaller assemblies have separate workspaces beside the engine.

Drag with one finger to rotate the active build. Drag with two fingers to move it across the view, or pinch to zoom. Only the assembly you are working on moves. Turn it until the target is visible; phone assembly works in any orientation and never requires a lift flip.

Use the Arrow button to point out the next part or fitting position. Next Step fits the next component for you. Captions explain the part and its function while narration plays. Chapters lets you revisit any section with earlier work already assembled.

Move within your safe play area, or use the left stick to walk. Push the right stick left or right to turn in steps. Push it forward to aim a teleport arc, then release to travel to the marked clear floor. The controller ray points at menu cards; press the trigger to choose one.

Point at a loose part and hold the grip button to carry it. Aim at the matching visible ghost and press the trigger for guided placement. Release the grip to put a loose part down. Each controller carries one part. Finish the active piston before starting another piston.

Reach for the red lift lever, hold the grip, and move the controller up or down to raise or lower its assembly. Release the grip to stop. Touch the red flip button, or point at it and press the trigger, to turn that assembly over. Each panel operates its own lift.

The captions and narration explain what each part does and where it fits. Press A or X to install the next part automatically. The left controller menu button opens the pause menu, where you can choose chapters, adjust settings, or return to the main menu.

Use the left joystick to walk around the garage. Drag on a clear area of the view to look around. The on-screen controls let you crouch, sprint and jump. Tap a part or lift control directly to interact with it.

Tap a loose part to pick it up. Tap matching parts one at a time to carry several in the inventory. Tap the matching visible ghost to fit the correct part. Complete one piston before starting the next. The captions describe the part's purpose and fitting position.

Hold a lift's red lever and drag up or down to change its height. Release to stop. Tap the red flip button when the narration asks you to turn the assembly over. Open chapters to choose a different section, or pause to adjust volume and placement difficulty.

In the display experience, choose Info and Timeline to inspect a part or play the assembly sequence. Engine Motion shows the working mechanism and its four strokes. The audio toggle silences timeline descriptions when you want faster playback. Assembly speed controls how quickly parts enter their fitted positions.
